summary: Defines a metric for variation in packet delay across Internet paths, based on differences in the one-way delay of selected packets. It works when the two measuring hosts have synchronized clocks and when they do not.

plainLanguage.summary: Packets should arrive at steady times. This describes a way to measure how much their travel times wobble, which matters for voice and video.

questions: what is ip packet delay variation
what is the ippm delay variation metric
does delay variation need synchronized clocks
subtitle: A precise way to measure how much packet travel times wobble, without needing perfectly synchronized clocks.

tldr.problem: People talk about network "jitter" but mean different things by it, and measuring delay between two hosts normally needs tightly synchronized clocks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines IP packet delay variation (ipdv) as the difference between the one-way delays of two selected packets, and builds a singleton, a sample and several statistics on top of it.
tldr.outcome: Because it is a difference of two delays, clock errors largely cancel out, so the metric works with synchronized and unsynchronized clocks. It sets no good or bad thresholds.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: Real number of seconds (positive, zero or negative) or undefined

facts.label: Minimum packets
facts.value: At least two in the stream

today: RFC 3393 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets no required values for delay variation; it only defines how to measure and report it.

sections.title: What Delay Variation Is and Why Measure It
sections.content:
RFC 3393 defines a metric for the variation in delay of packets flowing from one host to another along an IP path. It builds on the One-Way-Delay metric of RFC 2679, and the reader is assumed to know that document. The IP Packet Delay Variation, written ipdv, is the difference between the one-way delays of two selected packets in a stream going from measurement point MP1 to MP2.

The RFC names one important use: sizing play-out buffers for applications that need regular delivery, such as voice or video. For that, the maximum delay variation is what normally matters. Another use is studying how queues in a network or router change over time.

The metric deliberately does not define "good" or "bad" values. Any report of the metric MUST include all its parameters so that its meaning can be determined exactly.
sections.plainLanguage: Delay variation is how different the trip times of two packets are. A phone call needs packets to show up steadily, so knowing the wobble helps decide how big a waiting room to build.

sections.title: Why the RFC Avoids the Word Jitter
sections.content:
The RFC notes that jitter is used in two ways. One is the variation of a signal against a clock signal, as in synchronous circuits. The other is the variation of a metric, often delay, against a reference such as average or minimum delay. Because the word causes confusion, the document sticks to "delay variation" wherever it can.

It also defines relative offset, relative skew and relative drift for two clocks. Skew is the first derivative of the clock offset against true time, and drift is the second. The RFC notes that the maximum range of drift for commercial crystals is about 50 parts per million, mainly tied to temperature changes.
sections.plainLanguage: People use the word jitter for different things, so this document picks a clearer name. It is like saying exactly which kind of wobble you mean.

sections.title: The Singleton Metric: Type-P-One-way-ipdv
sections.content:
A singleton is one instance of the measurement. It is only meaningful statistically in combination with other instances. Its parameters are the source and destination addresses (Src, Dst), two times T1 and T2, a packet length L in bits (all packets in the stream MUST be the same length), a selection function F, an interval I1 to I2, and the packet type P.

The value is a real number of seconds, which can be positive, zero or negative, or it is undefined. It equals the one-way delay of the second selected packet minus that of the first. If one or both packets do not arrive, the result is undefined. At least two packets are needed in the stream.

The selection function says which two packets to compare. Examples in the RFC are consecutive packets, packets with given indices, or the packets with the minimum and maximum delay in the interval.
sections.plainLanguage: Send two packets and time each trip. Subtract the first trip time from the second. If one packet never shows up, you do not get an answer.

sections.title: How a Measurement Is Made
sections.content:
The method assumes synchronized clocks first. Starting after I1, the source builds test packets, for example following a Poisson sampling schedule. Padding should be filled with randomized bits, so that compression along the path does not make the delay look lower than it is. The source puts a timestamp in each packet, and the destination takes a timestamp as soon as possible on receipt. Subtracting gives a one-way delay estimate.

The first delay is recorded when a packet meets the selection criterion for the first packet. Then packets continue until the second criterion is met, or until I2. The ipdv is the second delay minus the first. If a packet does not arrive within a reasonable time, the ipdv is undefined.

Other rules from the discussion: if a packet is duplicated, the first copy to arrive determines its delay. If a fragmented packet is not reassembled, it counts as lost. The packet size must be reported, because delay depends on it.
sections.plainLanguage: Stamp the time on each packet when it leaves, stamp the time again when it arrives, and subtract. Do it twice and compare the two answers.

sections.title: Clock and Timing Errors
sections.content:
Two error sources are named: uncertainty in the clocks of the source and destination, and the difference between wire time and host time. Because ipdv subtracts two delays, a clock error that is about the same for both measurements cancels out. What remains is the difference between the errors at T1 and T2.

For linear skew, the extra error is the skew constant times the time between the two packets. The RFC claims that the effects of skew are rather small over these time scales. The resolution uncertainty is two times that of a single delay measurement, and the RFC says errors from accuracy and resolution are often larger than those from drift.

The host-time versus wire-time gap has a constant part and a variable part. Only the variable part causes errors, since the constant part cancels when ipdv is calculated.
sections.plainLanguage: If both of your watches are wrong by the same amount, the difference between two times you read is still right. That is why this metric copes with imperfect clocks.

sections.title: Samples and Statistics
sections.content:
A sample, named Type-P-One-way-ipdv-Poisson-stream, repeats the singleton over a stream generated by a pseudo-random Poisson process with average rate lambda. The result is a sequence of triples: the two send times and the ipdv in seconds, or undefined. Pairs should carry sequence numbers because packets can be lost, duplicated or reordered.

Statistics suggested in Section 4 include the distribution as an empirical pdf (a histogram) or cdf, a percentile, and an inverse percentile. Two named variants are an absolute-value measure called ipdv-jitter (the RFC says the term is deprecated) and peak-to-peak-ipdv, which pairs the maximum-delay and minimum-delay packet of each sub-interval. The RFC also describes the RFC 1889 jitter estimate, which applies an exponential filter with parameter 1/16 to the absolute ipdv values.

Lost packets leave ipdv undefined, so simple statistics such as the mean cannot be computed directly. One approach is to condition on the pairs that arrive, which means throwing out samples where one or both delays are undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: One pair of packets tells you little, so you repeat the test many times and look at the pile of answers, like the biggest wobble or the middle one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The ipdv metric has the same security properties as the one-way-delay metric in RFC 2679 and inherits its considerations. Three points are highlighted. First, someone could attempt a denial of service by sending many measurement packets, so legitimate measurements must choose their parameters carefully to avoid interfering with normal traffic.

Second, the packets contain no user information, so privacy of user data is not a concern. Third, attempts could be made to disrupt measurements by diverting or corrupting packets, and packet authentication and integrity checks may be used to guard against this.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurement packets should not flood the network, and nobody should tamper with them. They carry no private information.

items.title: Percentile
items.text: The Xth percentile of the ipdv values in a sample, where X is between 0% and 100%.

items.title: Inverse percentile
items.text: The percent of sample values less than or equal to a given value Y.

items.title: Jitter
items.text: Absolute values of ipdv for consecutive packets; the RFC calls the term deprecated.

items.title: Peak-to-peak
items.text: Maximum minus minimum delay in each sub-interval.
